utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Welcome back. We are hearing this week the Witness Nikolic, and I would like to state for the record his counsel is present, Ms. Virginia Lindsay. Welcome to our hearings as well. If there are no procedural matters? I don't think so. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. I was just standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You know your counsel, Ms. Lindsay, is present here in the courtroom, as you are a person in detention normally in another country and now transferred to the Tribunal. We are now commencing your examination. Mr. Thayer is putting questions to you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you again. Good afternoon to Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Defence. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My name is Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we'll get into the details of your military service in a little bit, but for now is it accurate to say that you served in the Army of Republika Srpska as chief of intelligence and security affairs in the Bratunac Brigade from late 1992 through the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to move things along a little bit, in May 2003 did you plead guilty to Count 5 of the indictment against you, namely, persecutions, a crime against humanity?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I pleaded guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in that earlier Srebrenica case, were the other co-accused named in your indictment Vidoje Blagojevic, the former Bratunac Brigade commander; Dragan Obrenovic, the former Chief of Staff and deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade; and Dragan Jokic, the former chief of engineering of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, the aforementioned officers from the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigade were in the same group together with me and we were all indicted together.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you'll pardon me, sir, I'm just going to adjust this ELMO because it's in our way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The court usher will assist you. You are perfect in technical matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I probably violated a union rule there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, following your guilty plea, sir, you testified for eight days in the Blagojevic trial in 2003; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly speak into the microphone, the left or the right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. I testified in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in 2009 you testified for another seven days in the Popovic trial and a day in the Perisic trial. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in addition to those cases before this institution, do you recall also testifying one day each in the so-called Kravica warehouse trial and the trial of Milorad Trbic in the State Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the state court I testified two times in two different cases, the ones that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I won't reveal your current location, but you testified via videolink in those two cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you are currently serving a sentence of 20 years' imprisonment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in connection with the guilty plea, was there a signed plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just take a quick look at the agreement and a couple of portions of it. We won't spend too much time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 7291, please, 65 ter 7291. And if we could call it up twice in e-court that would be helpful because the document itself contains a B/C/S translation. So I will provide both the English page number and the corresponding B/C/S page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, in a moment you'll have a document appearing on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we will need page 40 and 41. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the document that we have here has not been translated, but we're not going to spend too much time on this first portion. What we have here is the cover page of your -- the joint motion for consideration of amended plea agreement between Momir Nikolic and the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 42, please. And we'll need to go to page 49 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't know if you can read that, sir. Do you see what's headed "annex A" to the joint motion for consideration of plea agreement, amended plea agreement, do you have that in your -- on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. However, it's a very, very bad copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a little bit in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And enlarge it a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just paragraph 2 actually, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, we can see here that you pleaded guilty to Count 5 of the amended joinder indictment, namely, persecutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please, in each version and just blow up paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In B/C/S it could be enlarged a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you see paragraph 4 where it provides that in exchange for your guilty plea to Count 5 and your complete co-operation with the OTP as set forth in paragraphs 9 to 11, the Office of the Prosecutor agreed to, number 1, recommend that the Trial Chamber impose a sentence within the range of 15 to 20 years, and then 2, that the Prosecution would move to dismiss the remaining counts. Do you see those two provisions and do you recall those, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 45 in e-court and then that will be page 52 in B/C/S, please. And if we could focus on paragraph 9, please, scroll down just a little bit in the B/C/S so the witness can focus on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Under the heading "co-operation by Momir Nikolic" can you read the paragraph number 9, sir? Is it legible enough for you to read?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall that this portion of the agreement required you to accept responsibility for your actions, provide truthful co-operation and testimony in trials before this institution; do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, if we look at paragraph 11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll have to go to the next page in B/C/S only, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you see in paragraph 11, sir, that: "It is understood and agreed by Momir Nikolic and the Prosecution that all information and testimony provided by" you "must be absolutely truthful. And that this means that Momir Nikolic must neither minimise his own actions nor fabricate someone else's involvement." Do you see that and do you recall that part of your agreement, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see this document as well and I remember certain parts of this agreement. I remember what it contains in paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 7291.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 7291 shall be assigned Exhibit P2157. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, prior to the entry of your plea agreement and in fact prior to the finalisation of your plea agreement with the Prosecution, did you falsely state that you were present at an execution site and that you in fact gave the order for it? Do you remember making that false statement to the Prosecution during the course of the meetings in connection with whether or not you were going to plead guilty?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have already confirmed on a number of times that at a certain moment I stated something that was not true related to my involvement in the events in Kravica, and of course what I said at the time was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as the Trial Chamber just heard a little while ago, you've testified a number of times in a number of trials so I understand that you've told other courts about this incident as well as the balance of your testimony. But this Trial Chamber hasn't heard your testimony and you are here as a fully live witness. So can you please just give the Trial Chamber a little bit more detail, a better idea of exactly what transpired when you told the Prosecution that lie and took credit for a mass execution that you weren't involved with.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. As many times as I've testified here in The Hague, I've explained the situation which occurred related to me stating some things that were false, related again to the incident in Kravica. Of course this is a new Trial Chamber so I'm going to be very brief and explain what actually happened. The negotiations between the OTP and myself had already been well advanced. What I had to say in relation to my own involvement and the involvement of my unit and the involvement of others was something that I clearly stated. However, at a certain point the representatives of the Prosecution clearly asked me whether I had taken part in the incident in Kravica. And to be honest, I was afraid. I knew that I wasn't present, I knew that I wasn't involved in it, but I was confused. Those interviews took place of over a very long time and at a certain moment I was partially revolted by the situation, and on the other hand I simply didn't know what to do and what to say. So I said what I said and I took that responsibility. And then immediately after I said it I realised what I had done. I spoke to my lawyers. My lawyers definitely knew that I did not take part in that. And then the following day it was a public holiday in the Netherlands. I think it was the Queen's Day. And immediately after that holiday, I told my lawyers that I would want to tell the OTP that what I said was not true, that I would like to apologise about it, and that I would also take any responsibility for what I have stated falsely. There are some other details related to this, but I don't want to burden the Trial Chamber or to waste time here. If you have any further questions, if you need any further details, I'm prepared to answer all your questions. The essence of the matter is I have stated something that was false related to my involvement in the Kravica incident. Immediately after one day I apologised to the Prosecution and I accepted as a consequence of stating untruths to sign a true statement which will confirm that I have stated something that was not true in relation to that particular incident. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in fact, sir - and we won't need to take the time to put it up on e-court - but you refer to a signed statement which you made concerning this lie that you told. Did that in fact become part of your plea agreement package that was filed with the Trial Chamber in your case so that they could see exactly what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the statement. The statement that I signed was part of all the documents that were sent or submitted to the Trial Chamber. The Judges were aware and knew exactly what had happened because this was stated in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you understand how absolutely vital it is for you to tell the complete truth before this Trial Chamber and not to minimise your own conduct or exaggerate the conduct of anyone else? Do you understand how crucial that is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course I understand. In all my hitherto testimony I tried to be precise, of course within the boundaries of my intellectual abilities and within the framework of what I know. After the statement which I signed, I tried in all later or subsequent contacts with the Prosecution and in my testimony before the Tribunal to speak the truth. And of course it's absolutely clear to me - and I stated that in one of my statements - that I at no point wish to minimise my participation in the crime, while at the same time I also do not wish to bear responsibility of others or take upon myself the level of responsibility that does not belong to me in view of my rank and the position that I was in. And of course I'm going to try, in future testimonies also, to state all that I know, all that I saw, also in instances with my own participation and of course things that relate to my colleagues, officers from my unit, and officers from other commands about whom I know where they were and what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you pleaded guilty; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You accepted responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your prior testimony did you also express your remorse for what happened in Srebrenica and to the Bosnian Muslim population of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I testified -- actually, before the judgement was passed down I expressed my remorse and I do that whenever I have the opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, now is as good a time as any.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course countless times - and I said that earlier also - I expressed my regret about everything that had happened in Srebrenica. Of course I'm not only sorry but this is something that is troubling to me. After everything that happened I would like to take this opportunity again to apologise to all the victims. And since I was -- since I was a professor at school, I would like to take this opportunity to apologise particularly to my students who were victims of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, before you pleaded guilty and accepted responsibility and expressed your remorse, were you aware of any other Bosnian Serb army officer who had done that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I think I'm the first officer of the Army of Republika Srpska who simply understood that the -- who understood that the horrific crime that happened in Srebrenica is a horrific crime in which members of my army took part. When I say "my army," I'm not thinking only about my own brigade. And of course I think that in that horrific crime the things that I did in a way contributed to the events and everything that happened. Of course I testified countless times and stated that my role wasn't a crucial one, that I didn't plan anything, I didn't organise anything, that I didn't command the units, but the position that I was in meant that I carried out the orders that I received and that the operation ended the way it ended. I would be the happiest man alive had this never happened and had I never been there, but I was there, I saw many things, and I'm absolutely aware that a horrendous crime occurred there that cannot be justified in any way. And that is why as an officer of Republika Srpska, I pleaded guilty and I genuinely do consider myself guilty, I feel guilty, and I consider myself responsible for everything that happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to take a little bit of time and provide the Trial Chamber with a little bit of personal history about yourself, your education and your military background. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how old you are.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1955. I'm now 56 years old. I've entered my 57th year. I was born in that area, in that part of Eastern Bosnia. I was born in Bratunac. I completed elementary and secondary school in Bratunac. I completed the construction or engineering technical high school and then I went to serve my military term of duty the way it was served in the former Yugoslavia. I served my military term of duty in Slovenia. After serving my term of duty, I enrolled at the political sciences faculty and I completed the department of defence and security. After that I taught in school for a few years, and then sometime in 1986 or 1987 I moved into the municipal staff for Territorial Defence where I worked as a deputy commander of the Municipal Staff for intelligence affairs. This is what I was doing when the war broke out. That was my post. I was in the TO staff when the war broke out. And then in late 1992 the Bratunac Brigade was formed. After that, after a break that I had because of attacks against me by certain paramilitary formations in Bratunac, I was in Serbia for some five and a half or six months. I spent some of that time in the hospital. After that I went for rehabilitation and therapy. After that I returned to the Bratunac Brigade on the 19th of November, 1992, and some ten days after I returned I was assigned the chief of the security intelligence organ of the Bratunac Brigade. So since then, since 1992 until the end of the war, I was serving in the Bratunac Brigade. In late 1996 I moved to the Ministry for Missing and Displaced Persons, where later I became the co-ordinator of the Podrinje municipality on -- in dealing with refugees and displaced persons. I was doing that for a year. After that I became the director of a trading company, and then after nine months there the company was privatised and I was appointed as a director of another company. After that second company became private I was unemployed and I was arrested on the 1st of April, 2002 -- yes. Actually I was arrested on the 1st of April and transferred to The Hague on the 2nd of April, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's go back and just fill in a couple of details, sir. When you taught in Bratunac, can you tell the Trial Chamber exactly where you taught and which school, what was the name of the school, and what subject or subjects did you teach there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After I completed my university, I came to the high school centre. It's called Djuro Pucar Stari, it still bears the same name. And I was teaching defence and self protection or security there. This was the subject for first- and second-year students while I was working there, later things changed a little bit, but anyway my subject was defence and self protection which was a regular subject in the then-high school system.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were serving as chief of intelligence and security affairs in the Bratunac Brigade, what was your rank, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I had the rank of captain throughout my period of work in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you an active-duty officer, by that I mean a professional officer, or were you a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was a reserve officer, a reserve captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's spend a little bit of time talking about the Bratunac Brigade. I think you alluded to this earlier, but to the best of your knowledge when was the Bratunac Brigade actually formed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, could you please switch off your right microphone because it's too near to the keyboard which is in use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember correctly I think I said that it was in late 1992, but I think the correct date is the 14th of November. That was the day the brigade was formed. You don't need to completely rely on my recollection of the date, but I think that that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July of 1995, who was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The commander was Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how many battalions was the brigade divided into?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It had three battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were there any independent units within the brigade in addition to the three battalions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're thinking of precisely, but if you're thinking of a battalion that was part of the Zvornik Brigade then yes. If you're thinking of units that were part of the brigade, other units meaning -- that was the artillery logistics units, reconnaissance units, police, then it did include based on the establishment structure of a light brigade, all of those units that were planned for according to the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's what I had in mind, sir. And you referred to another battalion. Was there in fact another battalion that was, shall we say, affiliated with the Bratunac Brigade in addition to the three battalions that you described?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The translation is was there another battalion linked or connected with it. For a certain time-period another battalion was formed and mobilised. It has a provisional name, the workers' battalion or the work battalion, and it was established under an order by Commander Blagojevic at a time when it was necessary to engage all available forces for the Srebrenica operation. So if you're thinking of that battalion, the work battalion, that's its name. It was manned by conscripts that according to the war time assignments were deployed for work duty at work organisations. If you're thinking of a battalion that was our neighbour battalion, then it was the Skelani Battalion which actually was right next to the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of that Skelani Battalion, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think in all my testimony to date I recall a major. I think his name -- his last name is Petrovic, but this is not the Petrovic from the 3rd Infantry Battalion from my brigade. He had the same last name. I think the last commander in any case was a major. I don't have any other information about their command because they switched. Often people remained there for a very short time, meaning when they got there, when they saw what awaited them and what the situation was they would leave very quickly. But I think in May the commander of the Skelani Battalion was this Major Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade located?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade were in Bratunac some 500 metres away from the city centre. They were located in the premises of the Kaolin Bratunac enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in that command or in those headquarters, can you tell the Trial Chamber which staff organs were present?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This was a large compound with different buildings. So in those buildings and in a part of the compound the brigade commander was located, the chief of the brigade staff; then the deputies -- the assistants of the brigade commander, assistants for logistics -- actually, what I'm saying now -- actually, I'm not sure whether the commander for organisation and logistics was the commander of the Chief of Staff or of the commander of the brigade. This is something that I don't remember anymore. So the assistant for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs was there. Part of the command -- and the command had all the services, the traffic, the engineering, the medical corps, the logistics, also my office was located in that building and I was the chief of the security and intelligence affairs. There was also the staff HQ there. It was a minor unit which was providing security or actually it was doing all the things that were required by the actual command such as procurement, supplies, and other things. Also, outside of the compound in another part but that was also part of the Kaolin Bratunac enterprise was where the military police was located. It was a kind of prefabricated building that was next to the compound where they were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. And we will talk about the military police platoon in a little while. Sticking with the headquarters, was there a communications centre in your headquarters of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Trial Chamber just generally how did that communications centre operate? For example, how were communications from superior or subordinate commands received and processed in the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The communications centre was located in the same place where the HQ and the other organs of the brigade were, in the same building. The communications centre itself operated more or less as follows. Everything that was being sent from the brigade command would go to the communications centre. It would be encrypted there. It would either be sent encrypted or just plain text. And it would be information about the situation in the brigade, different information, as well as daily activities in the brigade. All of this was mostly sent in the form of a daily combat report to the superior command. My superior command -- well, not my superior command but the Bratunac Brigade superior command was the Drina Corps command. And everything that was new in the brigade and everything that was happening would be sent as a daily report at the end of the day to the corps command. The procedure was the same in all the communications centres. There were operatives in the centre who once you brought them the text or information that you wanted to dispatch, you would hand it to them, they would type it, dispatch it, and after that usually they would return the written copy of the text that you had provided to them in handwriting as well as the copy of the text that they had sent to the superior command. The practice in the Bratunac Brigade was as follows. The commander of the Bratunac Brigade trusted his assistants and other than special or exceptional information, he did not ask us to inform him each time that we sent some data or some information. He didn't ask us to submit to him what we were going to send. The next thing that I want to say is that we as assistants, again, after we sent out the information each time when we reported would orally inform our commander about our activities within our sector and the things that we had reported about to the superior command. When the situation was reversed, namely, when we received orders or any kind of document from the superior command then that would arrive at the communications centre and the complete document would then be taken from the communications centre to the desk. Perhaps this information arrived via post, not necessarily through the communications centre. So everything that would arrive in the course of the day, also from the superior commands, would go to the desk of the commander. If the commander was absent, he would be replaced by the Chief of Staff and the commander or the Chief of Staff would look at all the documents, all the instructions, all the orders that had arrived, and they would initial and pass them on to the relevant persons. All the assistants, for example, had their own codes. For example, I had 03, logistics was 04, operations was 06, and so on and so forth. The commander would look at the information, he would initial it, and then send it to whoever was supposed to receive it. And then also at the end of the day this would be dispatched to protocol. The person in charge of the protocol would distribute the documents according to what was written in the document itself by the commander. This is how the communications centre functioned in principle. I just want to add this. There are exceptions everywhere. Sometimes there are exceptions in the communications centre as well, but for the most part this was the procedure in the Bratunac Brigade, the way I just tried to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to follow-up on one thing you said, sir. You mentioned communications that were outgoing from the brigade, some which might be open text, others which were encrypted, and that that would be done by an operative within the communications centre. How about with respect to communications which were being received by the communications centre from let's say, for example, a superior command that were encrypted, what would happen then?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All orders that arrived at the communications centre would be decoded and converted into an open text. There was a specific person who was taking care of that. I myself am not very versatile in these matters, but in principle I know that every order that came from a superior command was converted into a clear, transparent, and open text. So it did not remain encoded, which allowed for a completely normal communication, if that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the communications centre, was there an operations room in addition to that communications centre or were they the same thing in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I more or less understand what you are referring to. The brigade had its communications centre, as I just explained. For example, in my brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, we also had an operations centre which provided daily operations duty, and now I'm talking exclusively about the Bratunac Brigade. In our operations centre, there was no communications system, there were no communication devices that would allow those who were sending something from the superior command to send it to the communications centre. Anything going out from the operations centre could only have been done by phone. There was an unscrambled telephone in the communications centre and there was also scrambled telephones. So from the communications centre this information can be passed on by telephone as well; however, all the information including orders could have been conveyed to the centre by telephone. As far as written orders were concerned, they were sent either by post or through the system that was established there for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think we'll hear a little bit more about both the communications centre and the operations centre or operations room during the course of your testimony. You referred to daily reports which were submitted by the Brigade to the Drina Corps. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether that was, number one, required every day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to the reports sent by a brigade, then you are right. That was done on a daily basis. A brigade was obliged pursuant to the corps orders to send daily reports to the corps command. And as far as I know our brigade complied with that in an orderly fashion. If you are inquiring about my sector, based on an agreement with my superiors in the area of professional expertise, we undertook an obligation to convey intelligence information or the information collected by my sector once a day, two times a day, or maybe even more because we wanted to inform the corps command about any changes in the situation that might affect the combat-readiness of our unit. If we didn't have such information, of course I was not obliged to write a daily report just to keep up with the appearances. I provided reports only when I had something specific to say and if this information was relevant for my superior command. So as I said, we sometimes sent two or three information and reports and sometimes we didn't send any at all. Therefore, since there is an item within every regular combat report that deals with security issues, I would usually just put one sentence to the effect that with respect to the previous report there are no new developments. And this is what I did in terms of fulfilling my obligations towards my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when we refer to the daily combat report that went up to the Drina Corps from the Bratunac Brigade, who would typically sign off on the daily combat report, the regular combat report that went to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A regular combat report should and must be signed by the brigade commander. However, it sometimes happened that the brigade commander was away and then that would be done by the Chief of Staff. Again, I'm talking about my brigade and the practice that we pursued was that the duty operations officer would, again depending on the content of information that has to be sent to the corps command, if this information is critical and important, then we did our best to show it to the -- our commander or the Chief of Staff. However, if these were regular daily combat reports and that contained no crucial information or any reference to any changes to the previous situation, then the duty operations officer would just add the word "for" and he himself would sign the report on behalf of the brigade command and then he would send it to the communications centre for them to type it and then pass it on towards the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, in your language the word is "za" for "for," is that correct, that we've seen so much of in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've referred in your last couple of answers to reporting through the command chain through the commander of the Bratunac Brigade as well as reporting obligations that you had to your professional superior officers in the security and intelligence line as we refer to it. In July of 1995 was the Bratunac Brigade an infantry brigade or was it a light infantry brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In July 1995 it was a light infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did that have any implications for your position as opposed to in an infantry brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A light infantry brigade had incorporated the functions of security and intelligence affairs in one personality. It is my duty to tell you that I'm aware of the fact that sometime in April or May - I don't know exactly - that these two functions were separated. We in Bratunac had a rather specific situation. The chief to be was first on the ground in Trnovo and then after that he attended some kind of course. So regardless of the fact that in that particular period of 1995 these two functions were separated, in the Bratunac Brigade nothing was changed in 1995 in terms that I was chief of the security and intelligence organ in the Bratunac Brigade. Later on when another officer came and assumed these duties, this question was no longer relevant for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately when this other officer came and assumed those duties? Month and year is fine if you can remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1995, but he was in Trnovo while Srebrenica operation was in progress. Therefore, I cannot tell you anything more precise. I can't give you any more details. And I also don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, during the period of let's say July of 1995 and the months leading up to July of 1995, day in and day out in the Bratunac Brigade who was exercising the duties and functions of chief of intelligence and security affairs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before July and after July, that is to say before, during, and after the operation, all the way until I left the brigade it was I who discharged the duties of the chief of intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of what your duties, responsibilities, and tasks were in your role as, first, chief of intelligence affairs in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'll try to explain this in two or three sentences, because basically all my responsibilities are described in the rules of service that pertain to intelligence and security and the work of security organs. These rules generally described what my rights and obligations were in the course of discharging these duties. So let me say about two sentences or three. The intelligence part of my duties, as far as I understood it, was the one that was the most important one that I was supposed to deliver. 80 -- or 85 per cent of all the activities have to do with intelligence and the rest, let's say 15 per cent, had to do with the activities that concerned command and staff affairs of my brigade. So I was not professionally involved in security. I was not an authorised security officer. I did not have a proper ID and I didn't have any powers that stem from that. I was mostly focused on intelligence tasks which involved collection of intelligence data about the enemy, about their activities, about their intentions, about their movement, and everything else that could greatly affect not the combat-readiness but rather the security of my unit and other troops who were within my units. So I said as far as the security activities were concerned, they mainly concerned the protection of one's own units, its weaponry and equipment, from incursions by sabotage or terrorist groups or the incursion of these groups into the rear areas of the territory controlled by my brigade. And this is basically what I was doing. As for the other tasks that were within the purview of a security organ who is working, for example, in an infantry brigade are quite different from the issues of security that I dealt with. That is perhaps the reason why I behaved in such a manner. Maybe I did not understand it properly, but nobody objected to that because this is how I perceived this function.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to yourself as not being an authorised security officer. What did you mean by that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is what I meant, of course according to what I know. Authorised security organs had a functional duty of chief of security. Authorised security organs also had official identification papers. This is how this was called in my country, and of course I had an opportunity to see this ID card and this ID card contains the duties of security officer according to the rules of service. For example, he was entitled to make arrests, to make searches. But, as I said, I was never performing these kind of duties and I wasn't permitted to do so because I did not have this kind of official ID that would entitle me to become involved in the security operations and matters. In our brigade in order for us to be able to deal with these kind of problems we had a different solution and that solution was a lawyer, a professional, and he was the one who dealt with the legal aspect of affairs relating to criminal reports and filing criminal reports and that is what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was his name, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: His name was Zlatan Celanovic and he was part of the organ for religious affairs and moral guidance only as a matter of form, but practically he was within the military police platoon and his authorities derived from the authorities conveyed by the brigade commander. So he did not operate only during the Blagojevic era, he also continued to do that when Slavko Ognjenovic became the commander, or maybe he did it even before. Anyway, he was always involved in these kind of matters until he was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the, if I'm doing my math right, about 15 per cent of your time was spent devoted to security affairs and you referred to the security of your unit. Can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about what does that mean? When you refer to the security unit, what does that entail in terms of your duties and responsibilities in terms of chief of security affairs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A while ago I told you that these activities referred to command staff affairs concerning security. That means providing security for the brigade command, providing security and preventing the leakage of secret information from the communications centre, and basically all other activities that affected the command and the staff of the brigade and their security of the brigade that I was a member of. If I may add, and I said that in my previous testimonies, I am not a security expert at all. I was mainly involved in my brigade in things that would contribute to the protection of the brigade and its units, and I undertook measures that would prevent putting the unit in danger or preventing any risk to the weaponry and equipment and other things that pertained to the unit and the area where it was deployed. So this was mainly my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did counter-intelligence fit into this scheme?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was within the remit of my sector and it normally does. And of course certain steps were taken with regard to these issues too, but unlike me the people who are trained in this particular domain know these things better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience what is counter-intelligence and did you ever deal with any incidents that you would characterise as counter-intelligence that you would recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot remember at the moment any particular activities in which I was involved that could be qualified as counter-intelligence activities. I really don't know. I can't recall. Maybe something would help me jog my memory, but anyway I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell us again what is counter-intelligence and does it fall under your intelligence hat or does it fall under your security hat?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, this has to do with security affairs. Certain security assessments need to be made. For example, with the potential intentions, with the degree of risk to which the unit or the area is exposed, et cetera. So as I said, I'm not an expert. This is how I understand it and I am reluctant to get involved in any deeper explanations. So within this scope of activities, I took all the measures that I deemed important for preventing any surprises or any incursions by sabotage and terrorist groups, the smuggling of fire-arms, illicit contacts between the soldiers on the lines, all other smuggling of contraband, et cetera. So whether you can call that counter-intelligence offices, I think you can, but I -- as I said, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we are at the appointed time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we must have our first break now. We will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've spoken about your reporting obligations to your superiors along the professional or expert line. Were there members of the Bratunac Brigade's subordinate units who also had intelligence and security duties? I'm referring to the battalions, obviously. Within those battalions, were there Bratunac Brigade members who discharged intelligence and security duties?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. All three infantry battalions that belonged to the Bratunac Brigade had assistant commanders for intelligence and security affairs within those battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what were their duties, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to repeat myself. More or less it was everything that I did at the level of the brigade. Those assistant commanders did the same thing at the level of the battalion within the zone of responsibility of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would they submit reports to you, whether oral or in writing, or would they report to somebody else with respect to intelligence and security matters?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The practice in my brigade -- or actually it wasn't just the practice, we had an obligation to do that. Intelligence and security organs in the battalion followed the same principle that I followed vis-a-vis my obligation towards the Drina Corps. So based on this principle they would send similar written reports to the Bratunac Brigade command, specifically to me within my sector for intelligence and security work. And maybe if I can add one more sentence. Following the same principle, if there was some important information that couldn't wait or that requested urgent action, then as far as the intelligence and security organs in battalion were concerned, they would always report to me. Of course it goes without saying that they would have to inform about it their own commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard testimony about on the one hand the command lines that we spoke about a little bit earlier running through the commander of the brigade as opposed to the professional or expert lines which in your case would run through the security and intelligence organs, both up and down through the subordinate and superior commands. Can you tell the Trial Chamber who was your immediate superior? To whom did you directly report?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the command and control chain, my immediate and direct superior was Vidoje Blagojevic, the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was your first superior officer when it came to matters of professional management and expertise in the field of security and the area of security matters?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior along the professional or expert line was the chief of the intelligence and security department in the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July 1995 who was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Performing the duty of the chief of security, and if I'm not mistaken about this, but I'm not 100 per cent sure, chief of security was Vujadin Popovic, while the chief of the intelligence sector was Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric. That's what I thought at the time, and I also think this right now, that as head of that sector it was Vujadin Popovic who was performing those duties.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphones be adjusted in such a way that it's sort of pushed to the left a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The court usher should assist the witness with the microphones, please. I hope it's now better for the interpreters. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of the sources of intelligence or security information that would flow to you, for example, up from the battalion level. What were some of the sources of that information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As I already stated, every infantry battalion had assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs. Information collected in the battalion were mostly directed towards what was going on in front of the front end of the battalion. Every battalion had its subordinate units, companies and platoons, and within those subordinate units they would have so-called observation posts. Those posts were manned by the observers from those subordinate units that comprised the battalion. So information about what was going on in front of their own units was collected in this particular way, by observation. Further on, in the Bratunac Brigade they had the practice of engaging reconnaissance units to gather intelligence information about the enemy activity. This means that those reconnaissance units would be sent into the depth of the territory to perform reconnaissance duties within the territory controlled by the enemy, that is the Muslim forces. General information of intelligence nature was also collected by interrogation of the captured persons and also by interrogation of the persons who switched sides. There were such people as well. So now I'm talking mostly about intelligence information that is important for the security of one's own unit and also information that could point to the forthcoming plans of the opposing side, I mean the Muslim side and their offensives or incursions of certain groups from their side. Such information would end up with the assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs at the battalion level, and then at the end of the day the assistant commander would forward this information to me. It was mostly them who would come because all those commands except for the 3rd Battalion were actually quite close. So they would literally come to me and tell me about it. Now, all this intelligence information that came into my hands came along this professional or expert line. Other information that would -- that certainly of the same kind would also go along the command and control line, which means that the assistant commander in the battalion would tell that things to his commander and then the commander would, along the normal reporting line, inform the brigade commander about this, which means that in his daily report he would provide a more detailed intelligence information of the same kind that I just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was there any priority in terms of to whom you yourself would report first when you had a -- for example, a piece of noteworthy intelligence information. Would you typically inform your commander first? Would you inform your professional expert superior officers first? Or can you not answer the question in that fashion and answer it in some other way? Was there any priority? Was there any rule that you followed with respect to whom you would first pass on this information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can only answer this question by telling you how I used to do these things. Everything that I received as new intelligence or everything that I planned to inform my superior command about, and especially if it pertained to the units of my brigade which it usually did, I would first of all report about all this to my commander usually verbally. Sometimes I didn't give any written reports to my own commander. And then immediately after that, if that was a relevant or urgent information, I would sit down in my office and write a written report to my superior command. By that I mean my expert organ which was the security and intelligence department within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And two related questions to follow-up on that, sir. This may sound very obvious to you, but what was the purpose of passing on this information, reporting on this information, for example, intelligence information, to your commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, my commander has to have all the information of this kind, I mean here the intelligence. That is the only way for him to make his decisions in a timely manner. He has to know what is going on or what is about to happen in order for him to pre-empt such things by introducing measures which will eliminate surprises or losses. So in order for him to make correct decisions about the future action, about the future behaviour, about the future engagement of forces, he absolutely has to have intelligence information, especially those related to the activities and intentions of the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the second related question is, again, what was the purpose of sending this type of information up your professional or expert line to Mr. Popovic or Mr. Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can answer in the following way. The corps command does not have just one brigade. The zone of the responsibility of the corps command is much wider than the zone of responsibility of the brigade. The zone of responsibility of the corps is comprised by the various zones of responsibility of the units which comprise the corps. So the corps commander can only make his decisions at the corps level, which is a higher level, if the corps command receives information from all the units which comprise the corps. So if the intelligence department receives information during the day from my brigade, from Zvornik Brigade, from Visegrad Brigade, then they are going to have a sufficient fund of information on which they can base correct decisions about future actions in which areas the corps command will have to put a special emphasis on their actions. So to put simply, based on the information that will reach the corps commander through the security and intelligence department of the corps, the commander will be able to make relevant, informed decisions about what will have to be done on that day or in some future period.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your work in the brigade and your experience in the war as chief of intelligence and security affairs, how did the reporting along the professional line, the expert line, proceed from the corps level up? Did it proceed in the same fashion that you've described from your battalions, to you, and then up to the corps, or did it proceed in some other fashion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can only speculate about how it was done on those higher levels. I can tell you that according to everything I know the reporting would have to follow the same pattern up to the very top; whether in actual fact it was like that, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about the military police platoon of the Bratunac Brigade. You told us it was in a separate building from the main command headquarters of the brigade. In July of 1995, who was the commander of the military police platoon?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The commander of the military police platoon in July 1995 was Mirko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was Mr. Jankovic's direct superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When speaking about the command aspect, the immediate superior to Mirko Jankovic was the Bratunac Brigade commander, Vidoje Blagojevic. When we talk about the professional line, the immediate superior of the military police platoon was I in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would, can you describe for the Trial Chamber the relationships between Commander Blagojevic and the military police platoon and your relationship to the military police platoon. You've described the command line versus your expertise line. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that means and how that actually operated in your experience on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What I want to say here is the following. The military police platoon is commanded directly by the officer of the unit or the institution within which the military police platoon is situated; specifically, in the Bratunac Brigade the military police platoon was directly commanded and controlled by the commander Vidoje Blagojevic. This as far as the command aspect. Vidoje Blagojevic in this particular case is the officer who makes all the decisions related to the use of the military police platoon. Now, speaking about the professional aspect, the officer who is the immediate superior of the military police platoon but only in the professional aspect is the chief of the security and intelligence organ of the brigade, and I was on that position in 1995. It was my duty to ensure that the military police platoon was always ready for combat, trained, and equipped and ready to perform police and other combat assignments. As for the engagement of the military police platoon and issuing orders about the use of the military police platoon, this was within the express jurisdiction of the commander. The chief of security or, more precisely, the chief of intelligence and security organ is the person who proposes the use of the military police platoon to the commander. So he says what he thinks about this use and how the military police platoon could be used in the most efficient and relevant manner. The commander does not have the duty to accept this proposal by the chief of the intelligence and security organ. So he doesn't have to but he could if he wanted to accept everything proposed by the chief of intel and security sector. He can also disagree with everything proposed and say, "This is what I actually decided." Once the commander announces his actual decision, all other discussion stops here, all proposals become irrelevant. Whatever the commander decides, regardless of whether the proposal was accepted in its entirety or just in part or not at all, he issues his decision. And after this decision is issued, I as the chief of the intelligence and security organ had the duty to enact whatever the commander decided. It means that it was my duty to ensure that the police carries out this particular decision in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I at this point in time put a question to the witness. To put it in non-military terms, would it be correct if I describe this in the following way. The chief of intelligence and security is responsible to prepare the military police for any action, the equipment, and the staff, and make proposals to the commander of the brigade; and the commander then is responsible to take decisions and to issue orders. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I understood from your question regarding the preparation of the police, the preparation and the training of the police is an ongoing assignment, meaning that the chief for intelligence and security has an ongoing duty to maintain full combat-readiness among the police, meaning that the police should always be ready to carry out military police jobs primarily and other military tasks that are commanded by the commander. That is the preparation of the police. If he so decides or if he says -- the commander can say that he would like to use the police in a combat assignment. I as the chief of police [as interpreted] - and this is how I used to do it - I tried -- actually, I did suggest to my commander what would be the best way in my view to use the police in the implementation of that particular military assignment. And after my explanation or my proposal the commander can simply accept everything that I stated, saying, "Yes, the police will be engaged in such and such an assignment in such and such a way." But the commander can also say, "Following my proposal that, for example, Mr. Nikolic, thank you for your proposal but I have decided to use the police in that way." When the commander decides to use the police force in a specific way, I have to respect that and I have to make sure within my remit that the commander's order is executed in the way that he planned. That would be the job of the intelligence and security chief in this professional aspect of managing the military police. All orders, all decisions along the command line go at the -- from the level of the commander of the military police to the brigade commander. The brigade commander is the one who issues final orders to the police commander and not to the intelligence and security chief. Once a decision is made, the order goes directly to the commander of the military police who commands the unit and carries out the task as ordered by the commander. This is how I did it in my unit. I don't know whether this is correct or not -- well, actually I think that this is all in keeping with the rules on the use of the military police. Command and control thus of the military police is regulated under Article 12 and then the following one defines the professional control of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Articles 12 and 13 relating to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is one point remaining unclear for me at least. You said you as the chief of security and intelligence were making proposals to the command of the brigade, and the commander would issue orders not back to you but directly to the military police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that he issued the orders to the komandir of the military police, not to me. Thus, that is the classic command and control of subordinate units. The immediate direct command over the police is in the hands of the police commander, but in the chain of command the direct control and command of the police lies with the superior officer of the unit that it is a part of. And this is defined in the rules of service of the military police Article 12. That is where it is specifically defined who commands the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you just referred to the immediate direct command over the police is in the hands of the police commander, who are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the military police commander, Mirko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did Commander Blagojevic have the right, the authority, to accept part of one of your proposals and reject others?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It's the discretionary right of the commander to accept or reject proposals. So yes, he did have the right to accept it or not to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience with Commander Blagojevic, were there on occasion proposals that you would make that he would accept in part and reject in part?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Rarely but it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just so we have a clean record, at page 36, line 25, and at page 37, line 1, Mr. President, there's a reference to -- we have in the transcript that the witness referred to himself as the chief of police. The answer is: "I as the chief of police - and this is how I used to do it - I tried -- actually, I did suggest to my commander what would be the best way in my view to use the police." I don't know whether we've got a slip of the tongue or just a translation issue or something else, but I just wanted to clarify with the witness whether he intended to refer to himself as the chief of police or something else in the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If it's in the transcript it could have been a slip of the tongue. It's me, I as the head of the intelligence and security organ. This is probably what I said or perhaps I made a mistake, but what I meant to say was I as the chief of the intelligence and security organ not as the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the brigade's military police platoon, was it further divided into subunits?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said "detachment." I heard "detachment." It's not a detachment. The Bratunac Brigade had a platoon of the military police. I apologise. The military police platoon numbered some 30 men. It was a classic organisation and there were three squads in one platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the three squads in this platoon that you just told us about, what were their duties, sir, day-to-day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were engaged mostly on shifts on the bridge, on the Drina. Then they had the check-point at Zuti Most, the Yellow Bridge, then they had their regular police duties. They had regular duty hours at the reception area before you would enter the brigade premises. And they also carried out regular military police assignments such as bringing in military conscripts that had left the unit wilfully and similar tasks which they performed as part of their regular daily activities. Oh, and I forgot one thing. They were also responsible for personal security for senior officers, the commander, and some other officers, for example, the brigade commander when these officials or officers were touring the units in the field. In other words, they were constantly executing military police assignments which at that time were occurring on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to responsibilities that may not have occurred every day or as frequently as these regular duties did, did the military police platoon have anything to do with prisoners of war or refugees?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can give you a general answer. All prisoners of war captured by the Bratunac Brigade and who were brought to the Bratunac Brigade were under the jurisdiction of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you aware of any responsibilities towards refugees that fell under your intelligence and security remit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Talking about prisoners of war, if I understood your question correctly, the duties of the intelligence and security organ and of the police was -- were to take care of the prisoners of war. Other than the duties that I mentioned above of the military police, they were also engaged on escorting military -- prisoners of war when this was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. In connection with your work as chief of intelligence and security affairs, did you use any particular rules or instructions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You mean professional literature or rules covering intelligence and security duties? If that's what you're thinking of, then I used books or instructions and rule books dating from the Yugoslav People's Army. These are mostly books dealing with intelligence support during combat. The one that I'm referring to is from 1977 [as interpreted]. I used also the rules of military police and also the rules of the security organ. I think that's what it's called now or something like that. In any case, all the rules that I used were rules that were used in the former JNA and we adopted them in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a quick look at a couple of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 390. I think this may also be D00203.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to greet everybody. On page 41, line 15, the year is 1977. I think that the witness said another year actually ten years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, would you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, the book that you referred to dealing with intelligence support during combat, what year do you recall that being published?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I thank the Defence for that intervention. And in the English if we could advance -- there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, on the screen we've got a cover of a book. Do you recognise what this is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the rules of service of security organs in the armed forces. And when I was talking about that earlier I said that I used this rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to another document, and this is P01297.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, are you tendering the document on the screen? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could just go a couple more pages in the original, please. And one more. And we'll need to advance in the English as well. It's going to be page -- there we go. If we could go one more page in the English -- I'm sorry, and one more in the English. It's going to be page -- actually page 2 in the English and if we could also rotate the page in the B/C/S when you get a chance, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've got a cover that's being blown up for you right now of another document. Do you recognise what this is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is rules of service of the military police. Your Honours, I would just like to say a word about what you asked me about. On the basis of this rule - which is the one that I used during the war - and in this rule of the military police is where what I was talking about earlier about command and control of the military police and the expert professional part of command and control of the military police is contained in this particular rules of service and this is what I was working under.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And actually, if we go to page 10 in the English we'll be looking at paragraphs 12 and 13, and in B/C/S that's page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you just referred the Trial Chamber's attention to these instructions, and we are now looking at paragraphs 12 and 13 of chapter 2 under the heading "Command and Control of the Military Police." Paragraph 12 states that: "The officer in charge of the military unit and institution within whose establishment the military police unit is placed or to which it is attached commands and controls the military police." Now, to tie this in to what you were talking about before, in paragraph 12 who are we talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 12 specifically means Commander Blagojevic and the Bratunac Brigade. Thus, Commander Blagojevic is the person who commands and controls the military police, the military police platoon, because that platoon is part of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 13 it states: "With respect to speciality, the officer in charge of the security body of the unit or institution within whose establishment the military police unit is placed or to which it is attached controls the military police. He makes suggestions to the officer in charge of the military unit or institution on the use of military police units and is responsible for the combat-readiness of the military police unit and the performance of their tasks." So in this paragraph, paragraph 13, in your brigade who does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 13, professional control of the military police platoon, that refers to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now if we could go to page 15 in the English, please, and I think this will be page 13 in the B/C/S. And -- sorry, my mistake. We need to go back because I want to catch the heading of this chapter and that's at page 12 of the English and page 11 of the B/C/S. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to take you to the heading of this particular chapter. We're going to look at a paragraph, specifically paragraph 25 of this chapter in a moment, but just for the record I wanted to put this chapter heading up. We can see it's chapter 3, "The Jurisdiction and Tasks of the Military Police." And then at number 2, if you can see number 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll have to go down, we'll go to the next page, I think, in B/C/S, unless it's right at the bottom or if we can scroll over maybe -- oh, it's a double page. Yeah, if we can scroll over to the right in the B/C/S I think we'll catch it. There we go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see number 2 is headed "The Tasks of the Military Police." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could go to page 15 in the English and page 13 in the B/C/S, please. And we'll need to focus on paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see that: "In addition to the tasks from items 22 to 24 of this rule, in war time the military police also execute the following tasks ..." And then we can see letters A through I. If we could focus for a moment on paragraph 25(f). Sir, do you see subparagraph (f)?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this refers to and how it falls under your remit as chief of intelligence and security affairs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure. It says taking part in directing the movement of refugees. In principle, yes, that was one of the tasks of the military police platoon, whereas the chief of intelligence and security organ in the course of preparation of documents and proposing measures to the commander suggests in which areas refugees and other persons should be rounded up. That is something that I know for sure, and I know that that was how it was done and that that was according to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And how about the second part of subparagraph (f) that refers to "... and uncover any members of enemy units who have infiltrated the refugees ..." How would that general task of the military police platoon fall under your role and responsibilities? What interest would you have in that? What role or responsibility would you have with respect to "uncovering members of enemy units who have infiltrated the refugees"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Let me tell you this. It seems to me this issue in the context that you put it is a hypothetical question. If you're asking me about specific dates, then we can speak about that. But as it is, I can say that it is possible and what is stated here is definitely one of the tasks of the military police when directing the refugees. As for the latter part of this statement relating to enemy formations infiltrating refugees, in theory that is possible.
