However, I think that infiltration by military personnel of refugee groups, I'm not quite sure that these things are happening in reality. A person who is fit for military service and is a soldier can be among refugees, it's all right. But a soldier with a rifle -- well, it's not quite clear to me why should such a person merge with the civilians who are going to be escorted by the military police and what was he supposed to do. So if we are talking about able-bodied men amongst civilians that is something which is quite normal and that is something that I myself witnessed in the aftermath of the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll talk about what happened to able-bodied men as you saw them after the fall of Srebrenica. Let's focus for a moment if we could on (h), subparagraph (h). What can you tell us about this paragraph in terms of how the military police platoon operated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The military police of course takes part in securing POWs and POW camps as well as other facilities for temporary detention of prisoners. The military police is only one of the segments or units or structures that in these specific cases would take part in securing the prisoners after the Srebrenica operation. So the role and the obligation of the intelligence and security organ is quite clear, as is the role of the police when it comes to physical security of the prisoners and the facilities in which they are detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at one more paragraph in these instructions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 21 of the English, and this will be page 19 of the B/C/S. And we'll be focusing on paragraph 54 if we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see part 4 under the heading or the heading "Escort Service" in paragraph 54 under that heading?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could also just read paragraph 55 to yourself and then we'll turn the page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could turn in the English we'll pick up paragraphs 55 through 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just let us know when you're ready to turn, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could turn in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this is about and how it relates to the activities of the military police platoon of the Bratunac Brigade in your experience.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, these two articles clearly show who is escorting whom and under whose orders. It demonstrates these kind of relations. In this specific case if we talk about the military police, after Operation Srebrenica escorted the captured Muslims or those who surrendered and placed them under the jurisdiction of the military police. They also had an opportunity to escort soldiers, members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that had been captured by the Bratunac Brigade; and roughly speaking, those were the activities relating to the prisoners. If it at all could be classified under this heading, they were also in charge of escorting and securing convoys that were travelling from Bratunac to Zvornik. So this is the widest context into which I can put everything that is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at paragraph 57, sir, it states that: "The military police may also, upon a special order, escort prisoners of war." And just picking up with what you were saying a moment ago with respect to what the military police platoon of the Bratunac Brigade was engaged in following the fall of Srebrenica, do you recall whether there in fact was a special order; and if so, who did the order come from? Or was there not a special order to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I can call it a special order when it comes to escorting POWs in the period after the fall of Srebrenica. In my opinion, that was an ongoing task that the military police platoon had at all times. The order to escort certain Muslim prisoners would be issued by the unit the part of which the military police was. And this order would specifically be carried out by the commander of the military police platoon. What I know is that the locations where the prisoners would be taken were determined by the corps command. So after the Bratunac Brigade inquired about the location where the prisoners would be transferred, the brigade command would receive orders from the corps command and then the brigade commander would issue a command to the military police platoon commander who would carry it out. If you would like to know what my role was on behalf of the brigade, I received a certain number of prisoners who were brought to the Bratunac Brigade HQ and I take -- took care of all the legal aspects of this process in terms of documents and papers. So the military police was involved in escorting the prisoners of war in this way as I just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we will definitely talk a lot more about what happened to the men who were separated in Potocari and the men who were captured along the road and brought to Bratunac and then taken up to Zvornik. So we'll have plenty of time to talk about that as well as other prisoners who were taken following the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we're done with this document, Mr. President, and I see it's already an Exhibit P01297.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned if I recall correctly that the battalions of the Bratunac Brigade had reconnaissance platoons within them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I am not sure that they had reconnaissance platoons. I may have said reconnaissance units, but as per establishment battalions have reconnaissance squads. So that's strictly as per establishment and also that was the situation on the ground realistically. Only one battalion had a reconnaissance platoon and that was the 2nd Infantry Battalion, but at the same time this platoon operated both as a reconnaissance unit and as a sort of intervention unit as they used to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And professionally speaking in terms of expert management, who would fulfil that role with respect to these reconnaissance units within these battalions in the Bratunac Brigade? Who would provide the professional or expert management of those units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the expert management at the level of the battalion, my answer would be that that would be done by the assistant commander for intelligence and security of the battalion. I'm sorry, I don't know if you asked me about the brigade or the battalion. I didn't hear you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, I think you understood me well, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber why the reconnaissance units would be placed under the expert management of the assistant commander for intelligence and security of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply for practical reasons. The assistant commander after the battalion commander is the second most responsible officer when it comes to the collection of intelligence and all other information pertaining to the area of responsibility of the battalion. In my earlier evidence I told you that one of the ways of collecting intelligence was by engaging reconnaissance units, whether it be in the area forward or even behind enemy lines. So that was the most compelling interests to do this, which is to have the reconnaissance squad directly connected to the intelligence and security organ and that is how it functions when it comes to my -- how it functioned when it comes to my brigade. If you allow me, Your Honours, I'd like to add just one thing in order to fully clarify the relationship between the reconnaissance squad and the rest of it. In units the functions of intelligence and security are separated. The reconnaissance unit is directly subordinated to the intelligence chief, whereas the military police is under the security chief. However, in my unit where all these -- where all these two functions were combined, the reconnaissance and the military police were directly linked to the chief for security and intelligence, whereas in the battalion it was directly subordinated to the assistant battalion commander for intelligence and security. I think that would shed some more light on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Nikolic, let's turn to a slightly different topic for a couple of minutes. I want to discuss another role or set of responsibilities that you had in the Bratunac Brigade and that had to do with your contacts with UNPROFOR. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what additional duties you had when it came to UNPROFOR, and particularly the DutchBat peacekeepers who were there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best. So in addition to regular duties within the purview of the intelligence and security chief, by virtue of an order issued by the Drina Corps command I was designated to act as a liaison officer between the Bratunac Brigade and in most cases members of UNPROFOR, but not only UNPROFOR, that included all other international organisations that were present in the enclave. I am specifically referring to MOs, Doctors Without Borders, and other organisations and of course when we talk about UNPROFOR I liaised with members of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you refer to the MOs, I take it you're referring to the United Nations military observers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you only need one microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you have counterparts in the neighbouring VRS units who performed this same liaison function as you were?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The neighbouring brigade was the Milic Brigade and the officer -- the Chief of Staff of the Milic Brigade, Sargic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was the liaison officer. Another neighbouring unit of the Bratunac Brigade was the Independent Skelani Battalion, and in the area of Pribicevac where the command of the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade is, and also the HQ of the Independent Skelani Battalion, there was the so-called forward command post -- no, I'm sorry, I meant the Pribicevac tactical group made up of - according to my information - Colonel Vukota Vukovic and his driver. That was the whole tactical group. Colonel Vukovic was an officer in charge of maintaining contacts according, again, to what I know with the other side on behalf of General Milovanovic [as interpreted]. However, all his contacts - I am talking about Colonel Vukovic - dealt exclusively with the Skelani Battalion and the Pribicevac area. Now, to summarise, in the group were Colonel Vukovic Vukota, Major Sargic, and Captain Vukovic, and we were in charge of liaison and we all had our problems that we had to resolve in our respective areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just noticing at page 53, line 7, sir, what we have here on the screen on our transcript is you saying that Colonel Vukovic was an officer in charge of maintaining contacts according, again, to what I know with the other side on behalf of General Milovanovic. I just want to make sure that that's what you meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think I said General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make that clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we're at the afternoon break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we must have our second break now and we'll resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, sir. We left off discussing your role as a liaison officer with DutchBat and the other international organisations. Focusing on DutchBat for a moment, please give the Trial Chamber an idea of the types of topics that were raised at meetings which you had with DutchBat representatives.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can only speak in principle about it and tell you the topics in general. The DutchBat, or rather, the representatives of the DutchBat and I spoke mostly about the problems that occurred within and without the enclave including the separation lines between the two opposing sides. Furthermore, we often spoke about their demands and the problems they were facing. We spent most time trying to solve the problems arising from the incidents between the two opposing sides. Specifically one of the biggest problems in this period while the DutchBat was present in the enclave were the problems related to establishing peace and order on the separation line and preventing incidents such as ambushes, excursions from the enclave, sniping of the enclave and the population within, as well as various ambushes, raids, and similar problems that were related to the separation line and the situation in the enclave and around it. So speaking in principle, this is it. If you have some specific questions, I can of course elucidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to ambushes, excursions from the enclave, and raids, what are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm going to speak now only about the separation line where the units of my brigade were engaged, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd Infantry Battalion, and later on in a certain phase a battalion from the Zvornik Brigade. So this separation line - I'm guessing now - but it was at least 20, 25, and even maybe 30 kilometres long. The part covered by the battalions from my brigade and later on, of course, the Zvornik Brigade. And on such a long line always, or rather, not always but very often you had incidents. Somebody would approach the line from the enclave, go towards the Serbian positions, open fire, sniper fire, and kill Serbian soldiers. Also on the other side - and I'm still talking about the zone of responsibility of my brigade - the Serbian Army had direct contact with certain settlements, including Potocari and other villages. And there were also -- there was also sniper activities, activity from the position of my brigade which would end up in wounding of certain people. A large number of this sniping activity was random and wanton without any specific target, which means that the targets were not only those people who had to be targets, people who carried arms, but also civilians who were tending their fields or maybe working around their houses. And in all these situations, regardless of the motive, the representatives of the Dutch Battalion and I would meet and then try to resolve those issues so that those incidents would be minimised.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall any of the DutchBat representatives complaining to you about raids that were bigger than, as you said, perhaps one Muslim soldier getting near a line and sniping somebody? Do you -- did you ever complain -- pardon me. Did DutchBat ever complain to you -- or -- sorry. Did you ever complain to DutchBat about larger groups of Muslim fighters leaving the enclave to target Serb targets outside the enclave? You spoke about cases where perhaps one Muslim soldier would engage in sniping close to the line. Do you recall any occasions when you complained to DutchBat about larger groups conducting raids or ambushes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can answer in affirmative. I complained every time when I had a reason to do so. I can quote individual cases right now. I remember some of them but not all of them of course. But of course whenever there was reason to complain, I requested the DutchBat to discuss those problems so that we could try to find a way to prevent similar occurrences, and there were cases like that indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You made reference in your earlier answer to the Zvornik Battalion. Can you just tell us what you were referring to when you mentioned the Zvornik Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the battalion which was engaged during a certain period of time around the enclave. I'm not sure about the exact time-period. I don't know the date on which this battalion arrived. I can only assume on whose orders it arrived. I don't remember the details. I know that they were engaged on a segment that was in a military sense rather unregulated. I'm talking here about the space between the Bratunac and the Milici Brigade. In that space between those two brigades, there was a certain area that was left uncovered. And of course that was before the Srebrenica operation when the Zvornik Battalion was engaged in this area and it remained there until the very end of the operation until the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were the soldiers from in the Zvornik Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I really don't know where they were from, but if they belonged to the Zvornik Brigade, then I can only assume that this battalion was manned by the personnel from the Zvornik municipality. I assume that they were military conscripts from that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when they operated in this space, were they resubordinated to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in command sense and in the logistics sense. They were resubordinated to the Bratunac Brigade. I know that they attended the briefings and I know that their logistics support was provided from the logistics base of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. During your contacts with the DutchBat representatives, did you make known to them what your position and function was in the Bratunac Brigade, that is, chief of intelligence and security affairs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, not really. I never told them what my function was. Sometimes we would joke together about it. They would try to guess what my function was and I never told them what my real function was. They thought that I was the Chief of Staff of the Bratunac Brigade and I didn't deny it and I also didn't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And -- sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: However, at the same time they didn't tell me their functions. They were not honest with me. I found that out only later. I didn't know exactly what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the reason that you didn't confirm or deny what your true function was in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. To be honest, I don't know that even now. I simply thought that there was no need and no reason to brief each other what exactly we do in our own units. I simply thought that to be honest that it would be easier to perform my work and easier to maintain those contacts if that was a little secret. It wasn't anything special really. I wouldn't be able to tell you even now why it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention now to the attitude of the Bratunac Brigade command prior to 1995 towards the Muslim population in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before I do that, though, I would just invite the Trial Chamber before I move into this new area we've covered obviously a lot of background, various issues concerning formation, duties, responsibilities, and if any members, Mr. President, of the Trial Chamber have any questions perhaps now is a good time. If not, I'll just keep moving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At that point in time there are no questions by the Chamber. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, prior to 1995 were you personally aware of any statements by the Bratunac Brigade commander pertaining to the Muslim population in the Srebrenica enclave and what the objectives of the brigade would be towards the population? And I'm referring here to Commander Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The interpretation that I received was whether I was aware of the statements, but since you mentioned Commander Ognjenovic I'm going to tell you that it is not about a statement but about information, a memo, wrote by Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic and that relates to the issues that you refer to in your question. Of course I am aware of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is a memo entitled information dating from 1994 written by my then-Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic. As far as I can remember, in this information he wrote an opinion about the situation in this area and among his views and positions there was also his view about the inhabitants of the enclave. He says that everything that could ensure that the life becomes unbearable there should be done. I'm now paraphrasing. I cannot give you an exact quote. He basically said that the life in the enclave should become unbearable so that the Muslims would leave the enclave because of that situation. Now, I don't know exactly on whose request and on the basis of what this information was written; however, I do know that Commander Ognjenovic drafted in a more detailed way this information together with the members of the command of the Bratunac Brigade, including the battalion commanders who attended that meeting. That means that all people present at the meeting were briefed about the contents of this information. And then after that Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic issued an order stating that every battalion commander should brief all other officers in the battalion on the contents of this information. After that, the company commanders should brief all the soldiers in the battalions which were stationed at the separation line. As far as I know - and I know this for sure - all members of the Bratunac Brigade, which means all the officers and all the soldiers, were briefed about the contents of this information which had been written before that in the Bratunac Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at this document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it's 65 ter 2364. And if we could have paragraph 1 in both versions blown up just a little bit, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you read it okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Based on what I can see in front of me, I think this is the information that I described earlier. This is the information dating from 1994 which was intended for the members of the Bratunac Brigade because here in the subject line you can see -- in the heading you can see the brigade name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can see that it's dated the 4th of July, 1994, and there's -- on the right it says "Jedinici" and something is written in there. Can you tell us what that means, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the 3rd Infantry Battalion. This is the abbreviation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 1 it starts out by saying: "During his recent visit to our Corps Command, the Commander of the VRS General Staff Main Staff indicated that he would soon visit some of the Corps units, including the Bratunac Brigade ..." And this reference to the corps command, what is that, sir, the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The corps command is the first superior command for the Bratunac Brigade, if that's what you're asking. It is of course superior to all the units within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July of 1994, do you recall where the Drina Corps command was located?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In Vlasenica as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July of 1994, who was the commander of the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The commander of the VRS Main Staff was General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we see in paragraph 1, and I quote: "This piece of information binds all units and brigade members to carry out all the preparations in commands and units regarding combat-readiness and to place it at the level our brigade is renowned for." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this is referring to, this passage here at paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can comment on what I can see here. The meeting was probably in the command of the Drina Corps and the commander of the Main Staff was present. I assume if I understood it correctly what you read out, he was supposed to visit, among others, the Bratunac Brigade as well. So all units are here ordered to keep the state of combat-readiness at the high level so that the commander would find a proper situation when he comes to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now if we could go to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S, please. And we'll need to scroll down in the English but we can keep the B/C/S where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you see in the original document where Colonel Ognjenovic writes: "We have won the war in the Podrinje but we have not beaten the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we need to go to the next page in the English only.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "We have won the war in Podrinje but we have not beaten the Muslims completely, which is what we must do in the next period. We must attain our final goal" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please scroll in the other direction again. We need the top of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "We must attain our final goal - an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde must be defeated militarily. "We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the Republika Srpska Army for the execution of this crucial task - the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave." Now, let me just stop there, sir, as -- the language that I just read out in this report, that describes what sounds like military action and as you stood as an officer of the VRS in 1994 and 1995 was there anything wrong with trying to vanquish enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I as an officer of the VRS see nothing wrong with militarily defeating the opposing side or as we called them the enemy side. This is a publicly declared military goal, and I can say as a soldier that there is nothing in dispute about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Ognjenovic continues in this document and it's on the same page in the original, the next paragraph he writes: "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave, we must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." Tell the Trial Chamber, sir, what this message is that's being communicated by Colonel Ognjenovic to the members of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You know, I could go on commenting this information for three days. I could give you comments on every word, every sentence. And in part I would agree with it and in some other part I would be absolutely opposed to what is written here if I didn't know what happened later with the Srebrenica enclave. However, since I do know what happened, since I know what problems I had because of this information, that is why I can openly say that I do not agree at all with a single word that we can find here that relates to the Srebrenica enclave and the activities that have to be performed. Why do I disagree? The reason is simple. During this period there was insistence on trust and co-operation with the DutchBat and the Dutch forces which were forces for the protection of the enclave. And our obligation - by that I mean the obligation that our Serbian side had taken upon ourselves -- and I would always talk about this obligation when I would come to meetings - was that there should be no change of the borders of the enclave, that there should be no attacks, that there should be no combat activities, that neither UNPROFOR nor the Muslims should be taunted, and I always insisted on that. On the other hand, you have a person who is my superior, my commander, and he writes a written document in which he requests that everything that I use to solve with the DutchBat has to be denigrated and he gives a green light to do everything that was forbidden in relation to the enclave. And you see that the goal is to make the life of the people in the enclave unbearable so that they would leave it as soon as possible. Now, I could understand and support Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic if he was talking about making the life of the enemy soldiers unbearable, if he was trying to do this in a military way. However, here this is obviously about the whole situation -- whole population of Srebrenica. This means that no distinction was made between the civilians in the enclave and others, and everything that was done also had negative consequences for the civilians. And that's the problem with this information. Here we can see that the violence was legalised, the breaches of the cease-fire were legalised, everything that was the reason for the presence of UNPROFOR was legalised. All those things that I used to discuss in the meetings. And I have to say to the Trial Chamber so that they would know, the person who wrote this, he's a politician. Before the war he never had any command, believe me. In my opinion, this is a political pamphlet, vulgar, and arrogant, and this was sent to all the units. But this cannot be justified. For me he was my commander at the time and there is no justification for saying things like that simply because he never held a command before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's go to page 6 and I'll ask you a few more questions about this document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's page 3 in the B/C/S. I see we're at page 6 already in the English. Thank you. If we can focus on the very bottom paragraph in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see just above Colonel Ognjenovic's signature and the stamp of the brigade it says: "Circulate this report among all Brigade members and have them sign for it. Review the report in companies, morale assistants are to introduce it in battalions while the Assistant for Morale, Religious, and Legal Affairs is charged with introducing it in the Brigade Command and Staff units, at the same time he will be held responsible for the accurate interpretation of this report at the Brigade level." Can you tell us how this language from Colonel Ognjenovic was treated. What was done pursuant to this language?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to the last paragraph, everything that is stated here and ordered here was implemented. Commander Ognjenovic wrote this information, then it was read out and debated at the meeting of the brigade commander with the brigade command and battalion commanders in more detail. That was followed by the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs preparing a copy each for battalion commanders. So the battalion commanders had this information and they reviewed it and analysed it in their respective companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was the distribution of this report to the battalions and the subordinate units treated as something that was optional, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that. Each information or each order that comes from a commander cannot be optional. That's how I understand it, and what I read from this is that this is an order issued by the commander about what is to be done with this information. As far as I know, it was mandatory for this to be analysed both at the level of the commands and the level of all the units and that is what was actually done. I am not telling you anything off the top of my head. I know exactly that this information reached the battalions and that they became familiarised with it. The consequence of this information was total lack of discipline along the separation line, the intensification of sniping and other incidents happened as a result of this information. I used to say that this information was just an alibi for the subsequent intensification of sniping fire and all other incidents that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that we're just a couple minutes away from the end of the day. I have a new topic. In the meantime, though, I'd like to tender this exhibit and it's 2364, 65 ter 2364.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness the following. We see here the name of Mr. Slavko Ognjenovic who signed this document. You said he was a politician if I understood you correctly, but we can see here that he was lieutenant-colonel. Was he also a military man or can you help me to understand this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I may have created a confusion here. Of course Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic was an active-duty military person. He was a brigade commander. However, before he came to the Bratunac Brigade he worked as a lecturer I think in the centre in Rajlovac. And according to what I know, he taught political subjects such as Marxism and things like that. So that was the reason why I described him as a politician rather than as a commander. One should make distinction between the people who used to be in command in peace time of battalions, companies, and other units and those who were indeed professional soldiers but did not hold any position of command of any unit before the war. And that is what I meant when I said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was indeed helpful. Do you recall when Mr. Ognjenovic was appointed commander of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. That was within the remit of the personnel service. He was appointed commander on two occasions, so I really wouldn't like to try and guess. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 02364 shall be assigned Exhibit P2158. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe I just refer to the person you described as a politician rather than a commander. Do you know if he was a trained soldier, military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that goes without saying. All active-duty personnel, military personnel, including the things that I know, I can say that Commander Slavko Ognjenovic was a military man who had finished the military academy. Of course he undergone certain training courses. However, I don't know what his speciality was and whether there was any subject that he particularly studied at the academy, whether he was focused or whether he majored in infantry or artillery or communications systems or whatever. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of April, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
